issues.subcategory: Confounded manipulation of memory decay
issues.description: The 'Short with Interference' condition in Experiment 1 conflates two distinct manipulations: temporal delay and visual interference. The authors treat these as equivalent ways to 'deteriorate' memory, but they may operate through entirely different mechanisms (e.g., masking of iconic memory vs. decay of working memory). Averaging over these two conditions to show a 7% increase in illusory errors obscures whether the effect is driven by time, interference, or both. The conditions should be analyzed separately and compared to each other to disentangle these mechanisms.
issues.quote: The interaction between Error Type and Memory Delay, (BFincl = 4.21) shows support for hypothesis 2: as memory deteriorates with a larger memory delay or more visual interference, the increase in illusory errors (7% increase from 19% in the short delay to 26% averaged over the short with interference and long delay) is larger than other errors (4% increase, from 8 to 12%).

issues.subcategory: Contradictory figure labels for Experiment 4
issues.description: The manuscript states 'Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials' in the Experiment 4 Results section, but Figure 5 is described earlier as belonging to Experiment 3. The figure depicting Experiment 4 data is labeled Figure 6 in the figure caption. This is a direct internal inconsistency that makes it impossible to know which figure is being referenced in the Experiment 4 results.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials. A Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA model comparison showed that the model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, Memory Delay...

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent BF reporting in Table 4 vs. text
issues.description: In Table 4 (Follow-up ANOVA for other, non-illusory error-rates in Experiment 2), the BFincl for Memory Delay is reported as 0.064, which constitutes evidence against including Memory Delay. However, the text states 'Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay).' This is a direct and severe numerical contradiction between the table and the narrative text—a difference of three orders of magnitude.
issues.quote: Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets (2% increase, from 10 to 12%, in both real and pseudo-letter targets).

issues.subcategory: High and differential exclusion rates with inadequate justification
issues.description: In Experiment 2, 92 out of 290 participants (31.7%) were excluded due to having fewer than 10 high-confidence trials in one or more cells. This is a very high exclusion rate. Critically, excluded participants had systematically lower high-confidence rates (15.7% vs. 49.2%), suggesting the exclusion criterion is not random but selects for participants who are more confident overall. This creates a biased sample and threatens the generalizability of the findings. The authors do not report whether excluded participants showed different error patterns, nor do they conduct sensitivity analyses.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the two color conditions. Included participants had on average 49.2% high confidence trial over all conditions (range: 24.6 – 95.8, sd: 13.3). Excluded participants had on average 15.7% high confidence trials over all conditions (range 0.4 – 38.8%, sd: 9.5).

issues.subcategory: High exclusion rate in Experiment 1 with inadequate justification
issues.description: In Experiment 1, 5 participants were excluded from the main analysis for having too few high-confidence trials, but the text is ambiguous: it states '45 participants started training, 5 participants were excluded based on their training results. The remaining 40 participants...all had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.' Then later it states 'Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded).' This means only 23 of the original 40 participants (57.5%) were included in the analysis, with 17 participants unaccounted for. The text mentions only 5 exclusions but the math (40 - 23 = 17) does not add up.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.subcategory: Confidence scale inconsistency across experiments
issues.description: Experiment 1 uses a 2-point confidence scale (1=guess, 2=certain), while Experiments 2, 3, and 4 use a 4-point confidence scale (1-4). The operationalization of 'high confidence' therefore differs across experiments. On a 2-point scale, any response above 1 is 'certain,' while on a 4-point scale the threshold for 'high confidence' is not explicitly defined. This makes cross-experiment comparisons of 'high confidence errors' problematic and potentially invalid, as the construct of 'high confidence' is not equivalently measured.
issues.quote: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain). [Experiment 1] ... and then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4). [Experiment 2]

issues.subcategory: High confidence threshold not defined for 4-point scale
issues.description: For Experiments 2, 3, and 4, which use a 4-point confidence scale, the authors never specify what threshold constitutes 'high confidence.' It is unclear whether responses of 3 and 4, or only 4, are classified as high confidence. This is a critical omission that prevents replication and makes it impossible to evaluate the validity of the primary dependent variable across the majority of experiments.
issues.quote: and then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4).

issues.subcategory: Insufficient evidence to rule out perceptual encoding errors
issues.description: The authors argue that because illusions increase over time, they cannot be purely perceptual. However, this logic is incomplete. Even if illusions increase over time, the baseline rate of illusions at the shortest delay could still reflect perceptual errors that were encoded into STM. The authors acknowledge this ('perceptual illusions can, at best, account for a small number of incorrect responses') but do not provide a principled method to quantify what proportion of the short-delay illusions are perceptual vs. memory-based. The increase over time is necessary but not sufficient evidence to rule out perceptual contributions.
issues.quote: This indicates that high confidence errors are not purely the result of errors in perception or encoding: when probed 0.75 seconds after the memory display has disappeared, people correctly report what they saw in 70% of high confidence trials, thus showing that initial perceptual encoding was relatively intact.

issues.subcategory: Response bias not adequately controlled in Experiment 1
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the target was a real letter in 75% of trials and a pseudo-letter in 25% of trials. Furthermore, the real letter counterpart appeared in the response display more often than the pseudo-letter counterpart. The authors acknowledge this but argue it is unlikely to explain the results based on the temporal increase in illusions. However, this is not a direct control—it is an indirect argument. A response bias toward selecting real letters (due to their higher frequency as targets and response options) could plausibly interact with memory decay to produce the observed pattern, as participants with weaker memories might increasingly rely on the base rate of real letters.
issues.quote: It is important to note, though, that throughout the experiment participants were more likely to encounter real letters as the target, and as the correct response option, than pseudo-letters, in line with the overall expectation that real letters are the standard letter-form.

issues.subcategory: Online data collection in Experiment 4 without equivalence testing
issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online via Neurotask, while Experiments 1-3 were conducted in laboratory settings. Online experiments introduce uncontrolled variability in display timing, screen resolution, viewing distance, and ambient lighting—all of which are critical for a paradigm relying on 250ms stimulus presentations. The authors do not report any checks on timing accuracy, nor do they test whether the online results are statistically equivalent to the lab-based results. This threatens the validity of cross-experiment comparisons.
issues.quote: Second the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time.

issues.subcategory: Post-hoc collapsing over cue color conditions without pre-registration
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the authors first tested whether cue color influenced illusory errors, found no effect, and then collapsed over cue color conditions for all subsequent analyses. This sequential decision—test a factor, find no effect, then remove it—is a form of analytic flexibility that inflates Type I error rates for the remaining analyses. There is no indication this decision rule was pre-registered. The null effect of cue color is also presented as a substantive finding ('expectations need substantial time to develop') without acknowledging that the manipulation check may have been underpowered.
issues.quote: First, we tested whether cue colour, and thus implicit expectations about the likelihood of real versus pseudo-letter targets, changed the number of illusory errors the participants made for real and pseudo-letter targets... Because of this, in subsequent analyses all data are collapsed over the two cue types (red and blue).

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration for Experiments 1 and 2
issues.description: Experiments 1 and 2 do not mention any pre-registration. The stopping rules for Experiments 3 and 4 are described (sequential BF analysis), implying the authors were aware of pre-registration practices, yet Experiments 1 and 2 appear to have been conducted without pre-specified hypotheses, sample sizes, or analysis plans. This raises concerns about researcher degrees of freedom in the design and analysis of the first two experiments.
issues.quote: Note that in this experiment the number of participants was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test [Experiment 3]... The number of participants was determined not by the experimenter but by student enrollment in the course [Experiment 2].

issues.subcategory: WEIRD and student sample limitations not acknowledged
issues.description: All four experiments used undergraduate psychology students from the University of Amsterdam, predominantly female, as participants. The effects depend critically on lifelong exposure to the Latin alphabet. The authors make broad claims about 'world knowledge' and 'predictive processing' as general cognitive mechanisms, but do not acknowledge that the sample is WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) and that the specific letter knowledge effects may not generalize to populations with different alphabetic experience (e.g., users of non-Latin scripts, or illiterate populations).
issues.quote: All experiments rely on the extensive experience participants have with the alphabet. Previous experience with letters should have provided participants with abundant evidence that letters typically appear in their standard form.

issues.subcategory: Mischaracterization of Fuzzy Trace Theory prediction
issues.description: The authors claim that FTT predicts 'high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories' and use this to argue FTT cannot explain their findings. However, this is a misapplication of FTT. FTT predicts that gist-based false memories arise from semantic/categorical similarity, not perceptual/visual similarity. The mirrored counterpart of a letter is perceptually similar but semantically distinct (it is a different symbol). FTT would not necessarily predict that perceptual mirror-image similarity drives false memories; it would predict that categorical membership ('this is a letter') drives them. The authors' refutation of FTT is therefore based on a mischaracterization of the theory.
issues.quote: FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory description of Experiment 3 results in Discussion
issues.description: The Discussion of Experiment 3 states 'people are more likely to have an expectation-induced illusory memory when the target was a pseudo-letter compared to a real letter' and refers to 'the same pattern of results as observed in Experiment 1-3.' However, this is self-referential—Experiment 3 is being compared to itself. More importantly, the discussion of Experiment 3 states the results are 'similar to Experiment 1-2' but then in the General Discussion states 'Experiments 3 and 4 show that pseudo-to-real letter illusory memories are also more prevalent than real-to-pseudo illusory memories when the stimulus set is completely balanced.' This is consistent, but the Experiment 3 discussion confusingly references 'Experiment 1-3' as if Experiment 3 is confirming itself.
issues.quote: As in Experiment 1-2, the results of Experiment 3 show that illusory memories occur in both real- and pseudo-letter trials, but, also similar to Experiment 1-2, people are more likely to have an expectation-induced illusory memory when the target was a pseudo-letter compared to a real letter... participants still show the same pattern of results as observed in Experiment 1-3

issues.subcategory: Missing details on how 'high confidence' was operationalized in Experiment 1
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the confidence scale is 1-2 (1=guess, 2=certain). The analysis focuses on 'high confidence trials,' but it is not explicitly stated whether 'high confidence' means a rating of 2 only, or some other criterion. Given the binary scale, this seems obvious, but the lack of explicit statement is a reporting gap, especially since the scale differs from subsequent experiments.
issues.quote: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain).

issues.subcategory: Accuracy rates not reported for correct trials
issues.description: The manuscript focuses exclusively on error rates in high-confidence trials but does not report overall accuracy rates, d-prime, or signal detection measures. Without knowing the overall accuracy, it is impossible to evaluate whether the high-confidence error rates are meaningful relative to overall performance, or to assess whether the paradigm was appropriately calibrated in difficulty. For example, if overall accuracy is very low, high-confidence errors might reflect a different process than if accuracy is high.
issues.quote: For each memory delay (short, short with interference and long) and each target type (pseudo- and real letter targets) the occurrence of illusory errors (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) and other errors (selection of one of the unrelated distractor items) was calculated.

issues.subcategory: Missing information on letter set used
issues.description: The manuscript states that symmetrical letters (A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y) were excluded, but does not provide the complete list of letters that were included in the experiment. This is essential for replication, as the specific letters used could influence results (e.g., letters with more or less distinctive mirror images, letters with different frequencies in Dutch text).
issues.quote: Therefore only letters that changed when mirrored were included in the experiment (i.e. the symmetrical letters A,H,I,M,O,T,U,V,W,X,Y were excluded from the memory and response displays).

issues.subcategory: Inadequate manipulation check for cue color expectation induction
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the cue color was intended to induce transient expectations about real vs. pseudo-letter targets (red = 25% pseudo-letter targets, blue = 60% pseudo-letter targets). However, the authors report that participants did not mention the color-target relationship in a post-experiment questionnaire, and the manipulation had no effect. There is no report of whether participants actually learned the contingency (e.g., via a learning curve analysis or explicit awareness check). The null result could reflect a failed manipulation rather than a genuine absence of transient expectation effects on STM illusions.
issues.quote: Participants filled out a brief questionnaire in which they were invited to indicate what the experiment was about after the experiment. The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses.

issues.subcategory: Overclaiming causal role of 'world knowledge' vs. stimulus familiarity
issues.description: The authors attribute the asymmetry in pseudo-to-real vs. real-to-pseudo illusions to 'world knowledge' about letter orientation. However, an alternative explanation is differential familiarity/fluency: real letters are processed more fluently, leading to stronger memory traces that resist distortion, while pseudo-letters have weaker traces that are more susceptible to any distortion. The authors address this alternative but dismiss it based on the argument that if pseudo-letters simply had weaker traces, all errors (not just illusions) should increase equally. However, this dismissal assumes a specific model of memory decay that is not independently validated.
issues.quote: Instead 'world knowledge' (e.g., which orientation letters usually have) appear to drive these STM illusions.

issues.subcategory: Training task uses different stimuli than main experiment
issues.description: The training task uses tilted rectangles (bars) in a change detection paradigm, while the main experiment uses letters in an identification/recall paradigm. These are fundamentally different tasks requiring different cognitive processes. The training criterion (75% correct on bar orientation task) may not be a valid predictor of performance on the letter memory task, and the training itself may not transfer appropriately. The rationale for using a different stimulus type in training is not provided.
issues.quote: Prior to the main experiment, participants were trained on a cued change detection task. In this training task, participants were instructed to indicate whether the rectangle at a cued location in a memory display had the same orientation as the rectangle at that same location in a test display.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent description of Short condition timing
issues.description: The Methods section states the memory probe appeared '0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display' in the Short condition. The Discussion of Experiment 1 states 'when probed 0.75 seconds after the memory display has disappeared.' However, the General Discussion states 'Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms.' The 500ms figure does not match the 750ms stated in the Methods. This inconsistency is repeated in the General Discussion, creating confusion about the actual timing of the short delay condition.
issues.quote: Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2) and up to 30% of reports when memory is probed at 3 seconds (Experiment 1-4).

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent short delay timing between Experiments 1 and 2
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the short memory delay is described as 0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display. In Experiment 2, the short condition is described as 'a blank screen...for 0.5 (the Short condition) or 3 seconds (the Long condition)' after the memory display, followed by a cue for 0.25 seconds. This means the effective delay to response is different between Experiments 1 and 2, yet they are treated as equivalent 'short' conditions throughout the paper and compared directly.
issues.quote: a blank screen, only containing the fixation cross was presented for 0.5 (the Short condition) or 3 seconds (the Long condition). Then the cue was presented for 0.25 seconds [Experiment 2]

issues.subcategory: Missing degrees of freedom and effect sizes for all ANOVAs
issues.description: The manuscript reports Bayes Factors but does not report degrees of freedom, F-statistics, or effect sizes (e.g., partial eta-squared, omega-squared) for any of the ANOVAs. While Bayesian analysis is the primary approach, the absence of any frequentist statistics or standardized effect sizes makes it difficult to assess the practical significance of the effects and to compare them with other studies in the literature that use frequentist statistics.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4, with the factors Target Type (real or pseudo-letter), Memory Delay (short, short with interference and long) and Error Type.

issues.subcategory: Overclaiming generalization to all STM stages
issues.description: The authors claim their findings apply to 'all stages of STM' including working memory and fragile memory, but explicitly acknowledge they did not test iconic memory. The claim that 'all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories' in the General Discussion is therefore not supported by their data, as iconic memory was not tested.
issues.quote: Our findings suggest that illusory memories can occur during the WM and FM stages of STM... Our experiments currently do not test whether illusory memories arise in IM... The fact that all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories has important implications for vision research

issues.subcategory: Irrelevant second display timing inconsistency creates confound
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the irrelevant second display appears at different times relative to the memory probe depending on the condition. In the Short condition, the second display appears 3.75 seconds after the probe; in the Long condition, 1.5 seconds after the probe. This means the second display could potentially interfere with memory consolidation or retrieval differently across conditions, creating a confound that is not discussed or controlled for.
issues.quote: If the memory probe appeared in isolation (the Short and Long conditions), the irrelevant second display appeared 5 seconds after memory display offset, which meant that the interval between the probe and the irrelevant second display was either presented for 1.5s (Long delay) or 3.75s (short delay).

issues.subcategory: Missing information on prior probabilities used in Bayesian ANOVA
issues.description: The Bayesian repeated measures ANOVAs are conducted in JASP, but the authors do not report the prior distributions used (e.g., Cauchy prior scale for fixed effects). Different prior specifications can substantially change Bayes Factors, especially for moderate effects. Without this information, the analyses cannot be replicated or evaluated for sensitivity to prior choice.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4

issues.subcategory: Lack of eye-tracking or fixation control
issues.description: The paradigm relies on participants fixating centrally while letters are presented around a fixation point. No eye-tracking was used to verify fixation compliance. If participants moved their eyes to specific letters (particularly pseudo-letters, which may attract attention due to their novelty), this could differentially affect encoding quality for real vs. pseudo-letters, confounding the interpretation of the asymmetric illusion rates.
issues.quote: Individual rectangles were evenly distributed on an imaginary circle (radius 4.68◦) around fixation.

issues.subcategory: Predictive processing framework not uniquely supported
issues.description: The authors argue their results support a 'predictive processing' view of STM. However, the results are equally consistent with simpler accounts such as schema-based memory, source monitoring errors, or signal detection theory (where weaker memory signals are more susceptible to response bias). The predictive processing framework is invoked as the preferred explanation without demonstrating that it makes unique predictions that distinguish it from these alternatives. The discussion of alternatives (FTT, differential encoding strength) is incomplete.
issues.quote: Our findings support a predictive processing view of the formation and maintenance of memory in which all memory stages, including STM, involve integration of bottom-up memory input with top-down predictions, such that prior expectations can shape memory traces.

issues.subcategory: Set size manipulation in Experiment 1 not fully analyzed
issues.description: Experiment 1 uses memory displays of either 6 or 8 letters, but the analysis averages across set sizes. Set size is a critical variable in STM research (affecting capacity and interference), and the authors do not report whether the illusion effects differ between set sizes 6 and 8. This is a missed opportunity to examine capacity effects and represents an unanalyzed source of variance.
issues.quote: The memory and cue displays were set up in the same way as the displays in the training session, with 6 or 8 letters replacing the tilted bars... Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.subcategory: Appendix referenced but not included in manuscript
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly references 'Appendix 1 for full model comparison' across all four experiments, but no appendix is included in the provided manuscript. Without the full model comparisons, it is impossible to evaluate the model selection process or verify that the best-fitting model was correctly identified.
issues.quote: see Appendix 1 for full model comparison and Table 1 for an overview of BFincl for each model component

issues.subcategory: Discrepancy in reported illusion rates between Results and Discussion of Experiment 1
issues.description: The Results section states 'when the target is a pseudo-letter, illusions are very common (37%)' as an overall rate. The Discussion states 'high confidence pseudo-to-real illusions (43%) were almost as prevalent as high confidence selections of the actual pseudo-target (50%)' specifically for the Short with Interference condition. These numbers are consistent with each other but the Discussion presents the 43% figure without clearly specifying it is condition-specific, potentially misleading readers about the overall illusion rate.
issues.quote: In fact, when the probe was after an interfering visual display, high confidence pseudo-to-real illusions (43%) were almost as prevalent as high confidence selections of the actual pseudo-target (50%).

issues.subcategory: Reinterpretation of De Gardelle et al. results without new data
issues.description: The authors suggest that De Gardelle et al.'s (2009) findings of perceptual illusions for mirrored letters could actually be memory illusions. While this is a reasonable hypothesis, the authors present this reinterpretation as if it is supported by their data. However, their experiments use a different paradigm and cannot directly test whether De Gardelle et al.'s specific results were perceptual or memory-based. This is speculative reinterpretation presented with unwarranted confidence.
issues.quote: However, the current research shows that this effect could also be due to a memory illusion: Perceivers might have seen the actual pseudo-letter, but just moments later remembered seeing the real letter. Moreover, Experiments 1, 2 and 4 show that this is perhaps a more likely explanation than an illusion that occurs when perceiving or encoding the stimuli
